questions.stem: Which Part and Articles of the Indian Constitution deal with Citizenship?
questions.explanation: Citizenship is covered in Part II of the Constitution, comprising Articles 5 to 11. Part I (Articles 1–4) deals with the Union and its territories; Part III (Articles 12–35) covers Fundamental Rights; Part IV covers the Directive Principles of State Policy — common distractor choices students mix up.

questions.stem: Under the Citizenship Act, 1955, which of the following is NOT a recognised mode of acquiring Indian citizenship?
questions.explanation: The 1955 Act recognises FIVE modes of acquisition: by birth, by descent, by registration, by naturalisation, and by incorporation of territory. 'Citizenship by investment' (a concept used by some Caribbean states) has NO place in Indian law. This is the intended 'exception' framing — the distractors name real modes.

questions.stem: Arrange the following Citizenship Amendment Acts in the correct chronological order of enactment: (I) 2019, (II) 2003, (III) 1986, (IV) 1992
questions.explanation: Correct chronology: 1986 (III, tightened citizenship-by-birth requirements after the Assam Accord) → 1992 (IV, permitted citizenship by descent through mothers, not only fathers) → 2003 (II, introduced the concept of Overseas Citizen of India and National Register of Citizens) → 2019 (I, CAA providing expedited citizenship to persecuted religious minorities from Afghanistan/Bangladesh/Pakistan). The distractors shuffle these.

questions.stem: Which Article of the Indian Constitution empowers Parliament to make any provision with respect to the acquisition, termination and all other matters relating to citizenship?
questions.explanation: Article 11 grants Parliament plenary power over citizenship matters — the Citizenship Act 1955 and all subsequent amendments draw their authority from this provision. Article 5 lays down criteria for citizenship at the Constitution's commencement. Article 9 says persons voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship cease to be Indian citizens. Article 13 deals with laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights — unrelated.

questions.stem: India follows the principle of single citizenship, unlike the United States which has dual citizenship (federal and state). Which of the following statements regarding Indian single citizenship is CORRECT?

options.option_text: Indian states can independently grant citizenship for residence-based purposes
A citizen of one Indian state enjoys fewer Fundamental Rights in another state
All Indians are citizens of India alone; no separate state citizenship exists
The President may grant separate state citizenship in emergencies

questions.explanation: The single-citizenship principle means every Indian is a citizen of India only — NOT of any particular state. This was a deliberate design choice by the framers to strengthen national unity (contrast with the US 14th Amendment's dual citizenship). Domicile-based benefits (like state university quotas) exist, but these are administrative — not separate 'state citizenship'. Option A is factually wrong; B contradicts Part III which applies uniformly; D is fiction.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem:
Match the following modes of acquiring Indian citizenship with their primary requirement and select the correct pairing:
(i) Citizenship by Birth  — born in India and at least one parent is an Indian citizen (post-2003 rule)
(ii) Citizenship by Descent — born outside India with at least one Indian parent at the time of birth
(iii) Citizenship by Registration — 7 years of ordinary residence in India (for persons of Indian origin)
(iv) Citizenship by Naturalisation — 12 years of ordinary residence in India for a foreign national

options.option_text: All four (i), (ii), (iii), and (iv) are correctly paired

questions.explanation: ALL four pairings are correct. (i) Post-2003 amendment: born in India after 03-Dec-2004 AND at least one parent is a citizen — more restrictive than the original 1955 rule. (ii) Descent: Indian parent at time of birth; since 1992 both parents (not just father) qualify. (iii) Registration: generally 7 years ordinary residence in India for persons of Indian origin (plus other grounds like marriage to a citizen). (iv) Naturalisation requires 12 years — 11 out of 14 preceding years, with the 12th year continuous.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) scheme is INCORRECT?

options.option_text: OCI status was introduced by the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003
An OCI card-holder enjoys the right to vote in Indian elections
OCI card-holders cannot hold constitutional posts like President, Vice-President or Judge
The PIO card was merged with the OCI card in 2015

questions.explanation: Statement B is INCORRECT — OCI card-holders do NOT have voting rights in India. They are classified as 'foreign nationals' and cannot vote, contest elections, hold constitutional posts (President/VP/Judges of SC/HC), or own agricultural land. Statement A is correct (introduced 2003 Amendment). Statement C correctly lists disqualifications. Statement D is also correct: the Government of India merged PIO cards into OCI cards through a gazette notification in January 2015.

questions.stem: The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 (CAA) provides an expedited path to Indian citizenship for members of certain religious communities from three specified countries. Which of the following is NOT among those specified countries?
questions.explanation: CAA 2019 covers migrants from Afghanistan, Pakistan, and Bangladesh who belong to Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, or Christian communities and entered India on or before 31-Dec-2014. Myanmar is NOT included — a frequent confusion given the Rohingya refugee crisis. The reasoning-distractor framing tests whether students confuse CAA's scope with general South-Asian refugee contexts.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Under Article 9 of the Indian Constitution, a person who voluntarily acquires citizenship of a foreign state:

options.option_text: Retains Indian citizenship unless Parliament terminates it
Automatically ceases to be an Indian citizen
Must obtain Presidential assent to retain Indian citizenship
Can hold both citizenships for up to 5 years

questions.explanation: Article 9 is self-executing: the moment a person voluntarily acquires foreign citizenship, Indian citizenship ceases automatically — no order, no Parliamentary action needed. This is distinct from termination under the Citizenship Act Section 9 (which covers the same ground statutorily). Option D describes no actual provision — India rejects dual citizenship; the OCI card is not citizenship. The 5-year option is pure fiction designed to trap students familiar with India's renunciation timelines for other regimes.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which ministry is the nodal authority for matters relating to Indian citizenship, including CAA implementation, OCI card issuance, and the National Register of Citizens?

options.option_text: Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment

questions.explanation: The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) is the nodal ministry for all citizenship matters — it administers the Citizenship Act 1955, issues OCI cards through the Foreigners Division, and oversees the NRC. External Affairs handles passports and overseas Indian affairs but NOT citizenship grants. Law & Justice drafts statutes; Social Justice deals with SC/ST/OBC welfare — unrelated.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 1986 raised the requirement for citizenship by birth. Under this amendment, a person born in India between 1 July 1987 and 2 December 2004 is an Indian citizen by birth ONLY IF:

options.option_text: Both parents are Indian citizens at the time of birth
At least one parent is an Indian citizen at the time of birth
Either parent is an Indian citizen and has resided in India for 10 years
The child is registered within 90 days at the Registrar of Births

questions.explanation: The 1986 Amendment (effective 1 July 1987) tightened the original jus soli rule: for births between 1 July 1987 and 2 Dec 2004, citizenship by birth required AT LEAST ONE parent to be an Indian citizen. The 2003 Amendment (effective 3 Dec 2004) tightened it further: at least one parent Indian AND the other not an illegal migrant. Option A is the post-2004 stricter rule incorrectly applied. Options C and D invent residence/registration conditions that don't exist.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Under the Indian citizenship regime, the 'termination' of citizenship (by order of the Central Government) is DISTINCT from 'deprivation' of citizenship. Which of the following is the primary distinction?

options.option_text: Termination applies only to women; deprivation applies to men
Termination is automatic on foreign-citizenship acquisition; deprivation is an order by government on grounds like fraud, disloyalty, or imprisonment abroad
Both terms mean the same thing — mere drafting variations
Termination requires Parliamentary approval; deprivation is Presidential discretion

questions.explanation: CORRECT distinction: TERMINATION (Section 9 of the 1955 Act) kicks in AUTOMATICALLY when an Indian voluntarily acquires foreign citizenship — no investigation, no order needed. DEPRIVATION (Section 10) is an order BY the Central Government on specific grounds: (a) citizenship obtained by fraud/misrepresentation, (b) unlawful communication with the enemy during war, (c) disloyalty to the Constitution, (d) a 2-year imprisonment within 5 years of naturalisation, or (e) 7 years of continuous residence abroad. A and D are pure fabrications; C conflates two legally-distinct mechanisms.
